subject: latin
title: 12 Aug — Cases & declensions
intro: Function first, ending second.
must: Genitive = of/possession; dative = to/for; ablative often = by/with/from or location.
Vocative = direct address. Learn a noun with its genitive to identify declension.

sections.title: How to identify a case
items: Ask who performs the action: nominative.
Ask who/what receives the action directly: accusative.
Check whether a preposition controls the case.

sections.title: Declension clues
items: The genitive helps identify the stem and declension.
Do not choose a case from word order alone.

sections.title: Common traps
items: A noun after ad is accusative.
A recipient is dative, not accusative.
Direct address needs the vocative form.

subject: latin
title: 15 Aug — Prepositions, agreement & pronouns
intro: Today is restricted to prepositions and agreement forms.
items: sub + accusative for movement; sub + ablative for position.
Adjectives/possessives agree in gender, number and case.
Check personal pronouns and all forms of ille.
must: ad, per and prope take the accusative.
sub + accusative = movement under; sub + ablative = position under.
Adjectives and possessives agree with their noun in gender, number and case.
Learn the personal-pronoun, ille and possessive tables as forms, not English word order.

sections.title: Agreement check
items: Decide its gender, number and case.
Make the adjective or possessive match all three.

sections.title: Pronoun control
items: Use the case to decide whether a pronoun is subject, object or recipient.
Do not assume ille always means only “he”; its form changes with gender, number and case.
Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner.

sections.title: Common traps
items: Do not omit the case governed by a preposition.
Do not use a nominative pronoun where an object form is needed.

subject: latin
title: 16 Aug — Perfect cues
intro: Learn the perfect cue with the verb.
items: Irregular cues still need exact recall.
Do not turn a present form into a perfect by guessing.
must: Learn every present cue together with its exact perfect cue.
-avi, -ui, -ivi and -xi are memory patterns, not rules that replace exact recall.
Irregular examples must be learned exactly: do not manufacture a perfect form.

sections.title: Safe method
items: Retrieve the learned perfect cue from memory.
Only then add the required perfect or pluperfect ending.

sections.title: Common traps
items: A familiar-looking ending does not guarantee the right perfect stem.
Spelling of the stem is part of the answer.
Keep present meaning and perfect cue separate.

subject: latin
title: 18 Aug — Four tenses
intro: Formation and recognition only.
items: Imperfect = was doing/used to do; watch -ba-.
Perfect = did/has done; use the learned perfect stem.
Pluperfect = had done; perfect stem + eram forms.
must: Present = present stem + personal ending: portat = he/she carries.
Imperfect = -ba- before the personal ending: portabat = he/she was carrying.
Perfect = learned perfect stem + perfect ending: portavit = he/she carried / has carried.
Pluperfect = perfect stem + eram, eras, erat, eramus, eratis, erant: portaverat = he/she had carried.

sections.title: Person and number
items: The verb ending tells you I, you, he/she, we, you plural or they.
Present model: porto, portas, portat, portamus, portatis, portant.
Always match the ending to the stated or implied subject.

sections.title: Common traps
items: Do not translate every past form as “did”.
Imperfect gives continuing/background action; perfect gives a completed event.
Pluperfect must mean “had done”, not simply “did”.

subject: latin

sections.title: Tense clues
items: Perfect: learned perfect stem and completed action.
Pluperfect: perfect stem + eram forms and had done.

sections.title: Common traps
items: Do not translate before locating the finite verb.
Do not ignore a preposition-controlled case.
Natural English comes after, not before, the grammar check.

items: English → Latin: subject, verb, object, recipient, agreement.
Latin → English: verb first, then cases.
Normal Latin word order can vary, but forms cannot.
must: English → Latin order: subject → verb → object/recipient → preposition → agreement check.
Nominative performs the action; accusative receives it directly; dative is the recipient.
Latin word order can vary, but cases, agreement and verb endings cannot.

sections.title: Worked source patterns
items: servus canem portat: servus = subject; canem = direct object.
servus epistulam fratri dat: epistulam = thing given; fratri = recipient.
ad hortum ambulat: ad controls the accusative hortum.
servus non tacet: non negates the verb.

sections.title: Production checklist
items: Assign the correct role and case to each noun.
Choose the verb person, number and tense.
Check agreement and spelling before submitting.

sections.title: Common traps
items: Do not translate mechanically in English word order.
Do not confuse direct object and recipient.
Do not omit non or a movement preposition.

title: 23 Aug — ad urbem
intro: Set passage only.
items: Perfect verbs move the story forward.
Do not import details from ad villam.
must: Storyline: Clemens and the others head into the frightened city; the streets are full of people escaping and searching; Clemens reaches the house; Quintus sends him onwards.
Perfect verbs move events forward: petivimus, intravi, audivi, perveni, misit.
Imperfect verbs describe background/continuing action: timebamus, currebant, festinabant, quaerebant, manebant, eramus.

sections.title: People and places
items: Many Pompeians run through the streets.
Sons and daughters look for their parents.
Metella and Quintus remain at the house.

sections.title: Translation control
items: Keep quod as “because” in these sentences.
Translate per vias / per urbem as movement through the streets/city.
Track ego, nos, me and te carefully.

sections.title: Common traps
items: Do not mix in the later temple episode from ad villam.
Do not turn imperfect background verbs into single completed actions.
Do not omit the reason clause.

subject: latin
title: 24 Aug — ad villam paragraphs 1–3
intro: Stop at paragraph 3.
items: Watch postquam, quod and movement phrases.
Keep completed events and background actions separate.
must: Paragraphs 1–3 only: panic, ash and flames; Caecilius and friends struggle through the streets; Iulius collapses; Clemens carries him to the temple; Caecilius promises Clemens freedom and runs to the house.
Perfect events: intraverunt, exclamavit, decidit, portavit, fecisti, servavisti, discessit, cucurrit.
Imperfect background: erat/erant, incidebat, petebant, complebant, contendebat.

sections.title: Key language
items: postquam = after; quod = because; tamen = however; subito = suddenly; statim = at once.
ad templum proximum = to the nearest temple.
tibi libertatem promitto = I promise you freedom.

sections.title: Translation control
items: Split long sentences at postquam and quod.
Keep commands separate from statements in Iulius’s speech.
Do not omit tibi in the promise.

sections.title: Common traps
items: Distinguish background danger from completed actions.
Track Iulius as the person Clemens carries and saves.

subject: latin
title: 25 Aug — ad villam paragraphs 4–6
intro: Paragraphs 4–6 plus comprehension.
items: Track who each pronoun refers to.
Do not omit tibi, tu, me, nos or mecum.
Answer from the passage, not memory alone.
must: Paragraphs 4–6 only: Clemens stays with Iulius; Iulius recovers and thanks him; they discuss Caecilius, Metella and Quintus; Iulius plans to leave; Clemens stays to look for his master.
Track pronouns exactly: tu = you, te = you (object), tibi = to/for you, me = me, nos = us, mecum = with me.
Do not omit the possessives meus/meum: they identify “my master”.

sections.title: Key language
items: postquam tu in terram decidisti = after you fell to the ground.
ego te ad hoc templum portavi = I carried you to this temple.
tibi gratias maximas ago = I thank you very much.
sine dubio = without doubt; quam celerrime = as quickly as possible.

sections.title: Speaker tracking
items: Clemens explains what happened and says Isis saved them.
Iulius thanks Clemens and criticises Caecilius.
Clemens refuses to leave because he is looking for his master.

sections.title: Common traps
items: Do not lose who “you”, “me” or “us” refers to.
Keep present dialogue forms separate from earlier perfect events.
